segments.text: At forty, everyone's arms get too short. <break time="350ms"/> So which reading glasses should you buy?

<sub alias="Eight hundred and twenty-six million">826 million</sub> people can't see well up close, for lack of reading glasses. In sub-Saharan Africa, only <sub alias="one point four percent">1.4%</sub> of over-fifties have their near vision corrected. <break time="150ms"/> Yet in trials, reading glasses raised productivity by <sub alias="twenty-two percent">22%</sub> and income by a third.
Small Print tells you which strength to buy, in two minutes, free, in your phone's browser. The camera becomes a ruler, and the video never leaves the phone.
Swipe the way the E points: no reading needed.
The E is redrawn about thirty times a second, so it always looks the same size to your eye. <break time="1500ms"/> Move away until it turns sharp.
Your answer: start with <sub alias="plus one seventy-five">+1.75</sub>.
If it can't see real eyes, it refuses to guess.
Then, at the shop, try the pair on: the app checks that your reading distance sits right in its sharp zone, before you pay.

Does it work? On <sub alias="two hundred and ninety-six">296</sub> real patients from published clinical data, it matched the clinician <sub alias="eighty-six percent">86%</sub> of the time. <break time="150ms"/> And unlike the standard age table, it held back readers from about half the short-sighted patients, who'd be harmed by them.

It runs serverless on AWS, for about <sub alias="sixty cents per thousand">60 cents per 1,000</sub> screenings. A coding agent built it through the AWS MCP Server, behind a guardrail that only lets it read. <break time="150ms"/> And AWS's own Well-Architected review found zero critical issues.
Small Print. <break time="400ms"/> Because everyone deserves to read the small print.
